passages.text: Observing this total eclipse from India, Jules Janssen saw a bright yellow line in the solar spectrum that turned out to belong to a new element, helium.

passages.title: Eddington's eclipse
passages.text: Expeditions to Príncipe and Sobral measured how the Sun's gravity bent starlight during this total eclipse, the first test of Einstein's general relativity.

passages.title: The last total eclipse of the millennium
passages.text: A total eclipse crossed Europe from Cornwall to Romania and on to India, watched by hundreds of millions.

passages.title: The Great American Eclipse
passages.text: The first total eclipse to cross the contiguous United States from coast to coast since 1918.

passages.title: The 2024 North American eclipse
passages.text: A total eclipse from Mexico's Pacific coast across Texas, the Great Lakes and Newfoundland.

passages.title: The 2026 eclipse over Iceland and Spain
passages.text: The first total eclipse visible from mainland Europe since 1999, crossing Greenland, Iceland and northern Spain near sunset.

passages.title: The great Egyptian eclipse
passages.text: One of the longest total eclipses of the century, with more than six minutes of totality near Luxor.

passages.title: GW150914: LIGO hears the first gravitational wave
passages.text: On 14 September 2015 at 09:50:45 UTC, the two LIGO detectors, at Livingston, Louisiana, and 6.9 ms later at Hanford, Washington, heard a gravitational wave for the first time, the first direct detection of gravitational waves: the chirp of two black holes, 36 and 29 times the Sun’s mass, spiralling together and merging into one of 62, 1.3 billion light-years away. Played as a story in four chapters: the black holes merging and their wave spiralling out through space; its journey to Earth, stretching and squeezing the planet as it passes; a ring of free masses showing what it does to space; and LIGO Livingston’s 4 km arms moved by the strain it measured, beside what both detectors recorded.

anchors.label: GW150914, heard at LIGO Livingston and Hanford

passages.title: GW170817: two neutron stars merge, heard and then seen
passages.text: On 17 August 2017 at 12:41:04 UTC, LIGO and Virgo heard two neutron stars, about 1.5 and 1.3 times the Sun’s mass and each some 24 km across, spiral together for about 100 s and merge, 130 million light-years away in the galaxy NGC 4993. A burst of gamma rays followed 1.7 s later, and a new light, the kilonova, was found 10.9 hours after: the first such merger also seen in light. Played as a story: the two stars orbiting ever faster, pulled out of round, and merging as their wave spirals out through space; a ring of free masses showing what it does to space; and LIGO Livingston’s arms moved by it.

passages.title: James Webb Space Telescope, since 2021
passages.text: A telescope in space, in orbit about L2. It sees visible light, infrared. The largest and most powerful observatory ever sent to space. Sees back over 13.5 billion years to the first galaxies born after the Big Bang. Mid-infrared views of dust and carbon-based molecules in star-forming nebulae. Operated by NASA; ESA; CSA.

passages.title: Hubble Space Telescope, since 1990
passages.text: A telescope in space, in low Earth orbit. It sees ultraviolet, visible light, infrared. The first large telescope in space for visible and ultraviolet light, and the first designed to be serviced by astronauts in orbit. Discovery of dark energy. First precision measurement of the expansion rate of the universe. First exoplanet atmosphere detected and its elements determined. Operated by NASA; ESA.

passages.title: Chandra X-ray Observatory, since 1999
passages.text: A telescope in space, in high Earth orbit. It sees X-rays. NASA's flagship X-ray mission and third Great Observatory, with the largest, most precisely shaped X-ray mirrors ever built, giving images 25 times sharper than any earlier X-ray telescope. Traced the separation of dark matter from normal matter in colliding galaxy clusters. Observed the region around the supermassive black hole at the centre of the Milky Way. Imaged the glowing remains of exploded stars and the dispersal of elements. Operated by NASA; Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory (Chandra X-ray Center).

passages.title: Planck, 2009–2013
passages.text: A telescope in space, in orbit about L2. It sees microwaves. ESA calls it the most sophisticated 'time machine' ever launched; it produced the most precise image of the cosmic microwave background. Most precise map of the cosmic microwave background. Age of the Universe: 13.8 billion years. Revised cosmic make-up: 4.9% normal matter, 26.8% dark matter. Operated by ESA.

passages.title: Gaia, 2013–2025
passages.text: A telescope in space, in orbit about L2. It sees visible light. It built the largest and most precise 3D map of the Milky Way, measuring nearly two billion objects. Showed the Milky Way's thick disc began forming 13 billion years ago. Revealed that our Galaxy merged with another large galaxy about 10 billion years ago. Measured the acceleration of the Solar System. Operated by ESA.

passages.title: Kepler, 2009–2018
passages.text: A telescope in space, in around the Sun orbit. It sees visible light. NASA's first planet-hunting mission and the first to find Earth-size planets in the habitable zones of their stars. More than 2,600 exoplanet discoveries. Showed the galaxy holds more planets than stars. First confirmed system with more than one planet transiting the same star (Kepler-9). Operated by NASA.

passages.title: Spitzer Space Telescope, 2003–2020
passages.text: A telescope in space, in around the Sun orbit. It sees infrared. The fourth and last of NASA's Great Observatories, and the first telescope to capture light directly from planets outside the solar system. First direct capture of light from extrasolar planets (2005). Revealed the TRAPPIST-1 system of seven Earth-size planets (2017). Found a huge new ring of Saturn (the Phoebe ring). Operated by NASA; JPL-Caltech.

passages.title: COBE, 1989–1993
passages.text: A telescope in space, in low Earth orbit. It sees infrared, microwaves. It showed that the cosmic microwave background has a near-perfect blackbody spectrum and produced the first 'baby picture' of the universe, earning the 2006 Nobel Prize in physics. CMB spectrum a nearly perfect blackbody at 2.725 K. First detection of intrinsic CMB anisotropy, at one part in 100,000. Detection of the cosmic infrared background. Operated by NASA (Goddard Space Flight Center).

passages.title: Herschel Space Observatory, 2009–2013
passages.text: A telescope in space, in orbit about L2. It sees infrared. The largest infrared space telescope launched before Webb, four times bigger than any earlier infrared space telescope. Revealed networks of dust and gas filaments where stars form. Traced water from star-forming clouds to planet-forming discs. Found Comet Hartley-2's water has nearly the same isotopic ratios as Earth's oceans. Operated by ESA.

passages.title: XMM-Newton, since 1999
passages.text: A telescope in space, in high Earth orbit. It sees X-rays, visible light, ultraviolet. The biggest science satellite ever built in Europe and, in ESA's words, the most powerful X-ray telescope ever placed in orbit. Used X-ray echoes to map the surroundings of a black hole. First sighting of hot gas sloshing within a galaxy cluster. Found hot, diffuse gas helping close the gap in the cosmic budget of normal matter. Operated by ESA.

passages.title: Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope, since 2008
passages.text: A telescope in space, in low Earth orbit. It sees gamma rays. It maps the gamma-ray sky from 8 keV to over 300 GeV, scanning the whole sky every three hours. Discovered the Fermi Bubbles, structures spanning 50,000 light-years. First light seen from a gravitational-wave event (neutron-star merger). More than 300 gamma-ray pulsars. Operated by NASA; U.S. Department of Energy.

passages.title: Compton Gamma Ray Observatory, 1991–2000
passages.text: A telescope in space, in low Earth orbit. It sees gamma rays. The second of NASA's Great Observatories and the first great gamma-ray observatory, covering six orders of magnitude in energy (30 keV-30 GeV). Found that gamma-ray bursts are spread evenly across the sky. Discovered blazars as the main source of the highest-energy cosmic gamma rays. Mapped the Milky Way in the aluminium-26 gamma-ray line. Operated by NASA.

passages.title: WMAP, 2001–2010
passages.text: A telescope in space, in orbit about L2. It sees microwaves. It produced the first fine-resolution (0.2 degree) full-sky map of the microwave sky and put the 'precision' in precision cosmology. Universe's age determined as 13.77 billion years, to within half a percent. Curvature of space within 0.4% of flat. Support for inflation from the pattern of density fluctuations. Operated by NASA.

passages.title: TESS, since 2018
passages.text: A telescope in space, in high Earth orbit. It sees visible light. The first spaceborne all-sky transit survey for exoplanets. More than 1,000 confirmed exoplanets. Nearly 6,000 confirmed or candidate exoplanets mapped by September 2025. Operated by NASA; MIT.

passages.title: IRAS, 1983–1983
passages.text: A telescope in space, in low Earth orbit. It sees infrared. NASA's first infrared space telescope, which made the first all-sky infrared survey and doubled the number of known astronomical sources. Discovered a disk of dust grains around the star Vega. Found six new comets. Revealed for the first time the core of the Milky Way. Operated by NASA; Netherlands (NIVR); United Kingdom (SERC).

passages.title: Hipparcos, 1989–1993
passages.text: A telescope in space, in high Earth orbit. It sees visible light. The very first space mission for astrometry, measuring the positions of more than 100,000 stars 200 times more accurately than before. Hipparcos Catalogue of 118,218 stars at the highest precision. Tycho Catalogue of 1,058,332 stars (Tycho-2: 2,539,913). Operated by ESA.

passages.title: Euclid, since 2023
passages.text: A telescope in space, in orbit about L2. It sees visible light, infrared. ESA's dark-Universe survey telescope; its NISP instrument has the largest field of view ever flown in space for an infrared instrument. First major data release covering more than a billion objects. Discovered 31 of the most ancient quasars, including the two earliest known. Operated by ESA; Euclid Consortium.

passages.title: Swift, 2004–2026
passages.text: A telescope in space, in low Earth orbit. It sees gamma rays, X-rays, ultraviolet, visible light. A first-of-its-kind multiwavelength observatory built to catch gamma-ray bursts and slew to their afterglows within about 90 seconds. First short gamma-ray burst with a detected afterglow (May 2005). About 1,800 gamma-ray bursts and 1,400 supernovae observed by its 20th anniversary. All-sky high-energy X-ray survey. Operated by NASA (Goddard); Penn State (mission operations).

passages.title: NuSTAR, since 2012
passages.text: A telescope in space, in low Earth orbit. It sees X-rays. The first telescope in orbit to focus high-energy X-rays (3-79 keV) into images. First precise measurement of a black hole's spin. Contributed to the first-ever picture of a black hole. Operated by NASA; Caltech.

passages.title: Spektr-RG (eROSITA, ART-XC), since 2019
passages.text: A telescope in space, in orbit about L2. It sees X-rays. eROSITA made the first imaging all-sky survey in medium-energy X-rays (up to 10 keV); its first catalogue is the largest collection of X-ray sources ever published. eRASS1 catalogue of about 900,000 X-ray sources, incl. ~710,000 active galactic nuclei and 12,000 galaxy clusters. More than 1,000 superclusters of galaxies identified. ART-XC all-sky survey (2021). Operated by Russia (IKI); Germany (MPE).

passages.title: Hale Telescope, since 1949
passages.text: A telescope on Earth, at Palomar Observatory, Palomar Mountain, San Diego County, California, USA. It sees visible light. It was the largest effective telescope in the world from 1949 until 1993. First official photographs taken by Edwin Hubble on 26 January 1949. Maarten Schmidt and collaborators identify the radio-loud objects 3C 273 and 3C 48 (quasars), 1963. Operated by Caltech (Caltech Optical Observatories).

passages.title: Hooker Telescope, since 1917
passages.text: A telescope on Earth, at Mount Wilson Observatory, San Gabriel Mountains, California, USA. It sees visible light. It was the largest telescope in the world from 1917 to 1949. Hubble finds a Cepheid variable in the Andromeda Galaxy (1923), showing galaxies exist beyond the Milky Way. Hubble correlates galaxy distance with recession velocity, confirming the expanding Universe (1929). First stellar diameter (Betelgeuse) measured by Pease and Michelson (1920). Operated by Carnegie Institution (Mount Wilson Observatory) to 1985; Mount Wilson Institute (current).

passages.title: Arecibo Telescope, 1963–2020
passages.text: A telescope on Earth, at Arecibo, Puerto Rico. It sees radio waves. When inaugurated in 1963 it was the largest single-dish radio telescope in the world. Demonstration of gravitational waves from a binary pulsar (Hulse and Taylor, Nobel 1993). First discovery of extrasolar planets (around a pulsar, Wolszczan 1992-93). Discovery of millisecond pulsars (Backer 1982). Operated by Cornell University (1963-2011, for ARPA then NSF); University of Central Florida (current manager for NSF).

passages.title: FAST, since 2016
passages.text: A telescope on Earth, at Dawodang karst depression, Pingtang County, Guizhou Province, China. It sees radio waves. It is by far the largest single-dish radio telescope in the world. 224 pulsars discovered by 30 September 2020. Passed national evaluation and began formal operation on 11 January 2020. Operated by National Astronomical Observatories, Chinese Academy of Sciences (NAOC).

passages.title: Very Large Telescope, since 1998
passages.text: A telescope on Earth, at Paranal Observatory, Cerro Paranal, Atacama Desert, Chile. It sees ultraviolet, visible light, infrared. ESO's flagship, combining four 8.2 m telescopes into Europe's most productive ground-based observatory. First image of an extrasolar planet. Tracking individual stars orbiting the supermassive black hole at the Milky Way's centre. Observation of the afterglow of the furthest known gamma-ray burst (at the time). Operated by European Southern Observatory (ESO).

passages.title: Keck Observatory, since 1990
passages.text: A telescope on Earth, at Maunakea, Hawaii, USA. It sees visible light, infrared. Their segmented 10 m mirrors made them the world's largest optical-infrared telescopes when built, and Keck II was the first large telescope to install adaptive optics (1999). Confirmation of the accelerating expansion of the Universe. Discovery of a supermassive black hole at the centre of our Galaxy. Spectrum of the most distant galaxy ever recorded (at the time). Operated by W. M. Keck Observatory.

passages.title: ALMA, since 2011
passages.text: A telescope on Earth, at Chajnantor Plateau, Atacama Desert, Chile (about 5000 m). It sees radio waves, microwaves. It is the most powerful millimetre/submillimetre telescope on Earth, giving images sharper than Hubble's at its wavelengths. Image of the HL Tau protoplanetary disc that changed theories of planet formation. Einstein rings imaged in extraordinary detail. Detection of complex organic molecules in a distant protoplanetary disc. Operated by ESO (Europe); NRAO / NSF (North America); NAOJ (East Asia); in cooperation with the Republic of Chile.

passages.title: Herschel's 40-foot telescope, 1789–1815
passages.text: A telescope on Earth, at Observatory House, Slough (demolished): about the corner of Windsor Road and Herschel Street. It sees visible light. For about 50 years it was the largest telescope in the world. Discovery of the sixth and seventh satellites of Saturn. Made the King's grant pay Caroline Herschel a salary as William's assistant, making her the first woman in England paid as an astronomer. Operated by William Herschel (funded by King George III).

passages.title: The Leviathan of Parsonstown, 1845–1914
passages.text: A telescope on Earth, at Birr Castle Demesne, Birr (formerly Parsonstown), County Offaly, Ireland. It sees visible light. It was the world's largest-aperture telescope from 1845 until the Hooker telescope opened at Mount Wilson in 1917. Discovered the spiral structure of galaxies, first recorded in the Whirlpool Galaxy (M51). Spiral structure then identified in dozens of other 'spiral nebulae'. Operated by William Parsons, 3rd Earl of Rosse.

passages.title: Yerkes 40-inch refractor, since 1897
passages.text: A telescope on Earth, at Yerkes Observatory, Williams Bay, Wisconsin, USA. It sees visible light. It is the largest refracting (lens) telescope ever used. W. W. Morgan's 1951 discovery of the Milky Way's spiral-arm structure (Yerkes Observatory). The 1897 dedication gathering formed the seed of the American Astronomical Society. Its photographic plate archive is used to study stellar motions and estimate dark matter in the Milky Way. Operated by University of Chicago (1897-2020); Yerkes Future Foundation (since 2020).

passages.title: Lovell Telescope, since 1957
passages.text: A telescope on Earth, at Jodrell Bank Observatory, Cheshire, England. It sees radio waves. When completed in 1957 it was by far the world's largest steerable radio telescope; it is still the third-largest. Tracked the rocket that launched Sputnik 1 within days of completion (October 1957). Received the first photograph from the Moon's surface, from Luna 9 (February 1966). Key role in pulsar research and tests of General Relativity. Operated by University of Manchester (Jodrell Bank Observatory).

passages.title: Murriyang (Parkes), since 1961
passages.text: A telescope on Earth, at Parkes Observatory, near Parkes, New South Wales, Australia (Wiradjuri Country). It sees radio waves. It is one of the largest single-dish telescopes in the southern hemisphere dedicated to astronomy, and has found almost half of all known pulsars. Prime receiving station for Apollo 11; received video of the first Moonwalk (July 1969). Almost half of the more than 2000 known pulsars found with it. Operated by CSIRO (Australia Telescope National Facility).

passages.title: Very Large Array, since 1976
passages.text: A telescope on Earth, at Plains of San Agustin, near Socorro, New Mexico, USA. It sees radio waves. One of the most productive radio telescopes ever built: 27 dishes on a Y, working as one telescope up to 36 km across. Quickly confirmed the first gravitational lens, discovered optically in 1979. Revealed for the first time a 'mini-spiral' of hot gas at the Galactic Centre (1983). Radar echoes indicating water ice in Mercury's polar craters (1991, 1994). Operated by NSF National Radio Astronomy Observatory (NRAO).

passages.title: Gran Telescopio Canarias, since 2007
passages.text: A telescope on Earth, at Observatorio del Roque de los Muchachos, La Palma, Canary Islands, Spain. It sees visible light, infrared. It is the largest optical-infrared telescope in the world. Key role (HiPERCAM) in discovering a ring around the dwarf planet Quaoar (2023). Detection of a possible 'fossil fingerprint' of the Universe's first stars in galaxy NGC 1277 (2026). Operated by GRANTECAN S.A. (Instituto de Astrofísica de Canarias-led; Spanish State and Canary Islands government).

passages.title: Subaru Telescope, since 1999
passages.text: A telescope on Earth, at Maunakea summit, Island of Hawaii, USA. It sees visible light, infrared. Its single 8.2 m mirror and wide-field cameras repeatedly set the record for the most distant known galaxy. Broke the 'most distant galaxy' record multiple times; at one point 9 of the 10 most distant known galaxies were Subaru discoveries. Discovery of Himiko, a giant gas cloud about 12.9 billion light-years away. Hyper Suprime-Cam survey found about 200 protoclusters of galaxies about 12 billion light-years away. Operated by National Astronomical Observatory of Japan (NAOJ), NINS.

passages.title: Vera C. Rubin Observatory, since 2025
passages.text: A telescope on Earth, at Cerro Pachón, Chile. It sees visible light. It carries the largest digital camera ever built and is running the 10-year Legacy Survey of Space and Time. 2104 never-before-seen asteroids discovered in about 10 hours of First Look observations, including seven near-Earth asteroids. First Look images (23 June 2025) of the Trifid and Lagoon nebulae and the Virgo Cluster, showing about 10 million galaxies. Operated by NSF NOIRLab; SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory (DOE).

passages.title: Extremely Large Telescope, being built since 2014
passages.text: A telescope on Earth, at Cerro Armazones (3046 m), Atacama Desert, Chile. It sees visible light, infrared. When complete it will be the world's biggest eye on the sky. Operated by European Southern Observatory (ESO).

passages.title: SKA-Low, being built since 2021
passages.text: A telescope on Earth, at Inyarrimanha Ilgari Bundara, Murchison, Western Australia. It sees radio waves. Being built as one of the two SKA telescopes: the low-frequency array, in Western Australia. Operated by SKA Observatory.

passages.title: SKA-Mid, being built since 2021
passages.text: A telescope on Earth, at Karoo, Northern Cape, South Africa. It sees radio waves. Being built as one of the two SKA telescopes: the mid-frequency array of dishes, in South Africa. Operated by SKA Observatory.

passages.title: End-Ordovician mass extinction
passages.text: One of the four marine extinctions that stand apart in the fossil record, in two pulses. An ice age over Gondwana, then at the South Pole: the first pulse came as the ice grew and the seas cooled and fell, the second as it melted and oxygen-poor water spread. Not one cause but several together. The usual “Big Five” come from Raup & Sepkoski (1982), who found the Devonian’s stands out but not significantly. Bambach (2006) finds only three stand apart from the rest; Rampino & Shen (2019) add the end-Guadalupian as a sixth. Warm seas, and ice in the south. Late in the Ordovician the tropical seas are 32 to 37 °C, yet ice sheets already cover much of Gondwana, then over the South Pole. The first pulse: the ice at its greatest? It is argued. The tropics cool by about 5 °C, the ice grows at least as large as in the last ice age, and the seas fall; many groups lose their habitats and die out (Finnegan et al.; Harper et al.). Bond & Grasby read it otherwise: mercury from an unknown large volcanic province, warming and oxygen-poor water, not the cold, drove both pulses. The second pulse: warming, and water without oxygen. A million years later, as the ice melts, oxygen-poor water spreads from the deep onto the shelves and productivity collapses. Between the two pulses some 85% of species are gone. Into the Silurian. Ice lingers into the early Silurian, but never again as large; the survivors rebuild the seas’ life.

passages.title: Late Devonian extinction
passages.text: Reefs and the life of warm shallow seas were hit hardest. Argued. Pulses of oxygen-poor seas, the Kellwasser black shales (Bond & Wignall); tropical seas cooling by 5–7 °C (Joachimski & Buggisch); the new forests’ soils feeding the seas with nutrients (Algeo & Scheckler); the Viluy Traps, erupting in Siberia near the time (Ricci et al.). The usual “Big Five” come from Raup & Sepkoski (1982), who found the Devonian’s stands out but not significantly. Bambach (2006) finds only three stand apart from the rest; Rampino & Shen (2019) add the end-Guadalupian as a sixth. The first forests. Trees and seed plants spread over the land, their deeper roots and soils speeding weathering and washing nutrients into the seas: a long Devonian crisis for the tropical reefs is under way. Volcanoes? It is argued. Mercury enriched worldwide points to volcanism, the Viluy Traps in Siberia the usual suspect, dated near the crisis; how it drove the changes is still more question than answer. The lower Kellwasser: oxygen-poor seas. The sea rises, and water without oxygen spreads over the shelves, leaving black shales. The tropics cool. Twice the tropical seas cool by 5 to 7 °C as carbon is buried and CO₂ falls; the warm shallow seas’ life, used to the heat, suffers most. The upper Kellwasser: the reefs collapse. 600,000 years after the first, the second pulse of oxygen-poor water, at the Frasnian–Famennian boundary. Its timing follows Earth’s orbit, as in later crises: the reef builders are hit hardest.

passages.title: End-Guadalupian extinction
passages.text: Put forward as a sixth great extinction, by the genera lost and its effect on ecosystems. In southwest China the Emeishan lavas lie among the limestones that record it: the eruptions began as the extinction did. The usual “Big Five” come from Raup & Sepkoski (1982), who found the Devonian’s stands out but not significantly. Bambach (2006) finds only three stand apart from the rest; Rampino & Shen (2019) add the end-Guadalupian as a sixth. A sixth great extinction? It is argued. Late in the Middle Permian, eight million years before the end-Permian. Usually left out of the five, it is put forward as a sixth by the genera lost, and above all by its effect on ecosystems. Eruptions into the sea, and the extinction. In southwest China the first Emeishan eruptions explode through the sea as steam and ash, and in the same rocks the large foraminifers and calcareous algae die out with them. The carbon cycle upset. Only after the extinction does a large shift in carbon isotopes come, a sign of the carbon cycle severely disturbed. The flood basalts. The Emeishan basalts cover some 300,000 km² of the Yangtze Block’s western margin, erupted within three million years at most.

anchors.label: Emeishan Traps, Sichuan, 259.8 million years ago

passages.title: End-Permian mass extinction: the Great Dying
passages.text: The most severe known, in at most 61,000 ± 48,000 years: more than 90% of the sea’s species and 75% of the land’s, as usually quoted (Burgess & Bowring); some 81% of the sea’s once the extinction already under way before it is counted apart (Stanley). The Siberian Traps, erupting before, during and after it. As it began, their sills spread through coal and evaporites, and the heat released greenhouse gases and halocarbons through hundreds of vents. The usual “Big Five” come from Raup & Sepkoski (1982), who found the Devonian’s stands out but not significantly. Bambach (2006) finds only three stand apart from the rest; Rampino & Shen (2019) add the end-Guadalupian as a sixth. On land, earlier? It is argued. Pangaea, late in the Permian. In Australia the Glossopteris forests collapsed before 252.3 million years ago, some 370,000 years before the sea’s extinction (Fielding et al.); in South Africa’s Karoo the change of animals long held to mark it is over 300,000 years older too (Gastaldo et al.). The usual view had land and sea dying together. The Siberian Traps erupt. Flood lavas pour over Siberia, among the largest eruptions since animals arose. About two thirds of them come out before and during the extinction, over some 300,000 years. The seas warm. Just before the main extinction, the tropical sea’s surface warms by about 8 °C, as light carbon from the Siberian Traps and what they heated pours into the air. Sills bake the rocks: the gas. As the extinction begins, the magma spreads underground in sills through coal and evaporites, and the heat drives off carbon dioxide, methane and halocarbons through hundreds of vents; sulfur, chlorine and fluorine come with the magma itself. The Great Dying. In at most 61,000 ± 48,000 years, more than 90% of the sea’s species and 75% of the land’s are lost, as usually quoted; some 81% of the sea’s once the extinction already under way is counted apart (Stanley). In the sea, heat and loss of oxygen together explain most of the losses, and where they fell hardest. The oceans acidify. The first pulse of extinction came with a slow release of carbon, and the sea’s pH held. In the second, a rapid, large release acidified the sea abruptly, killing above all the life with heavy shells. Six times the carbon dioxide, or thirteen? It is argued. From fossil plants, carbon dioxide rises from some 430 to some 2,500 ppm within about 75,000 years, and the volcanoes’ own gas was probably not enough: carbon from organic matter and methane, which the Siberian Traps released, was likely needed too (Wu et al.). From an Earth-system model fitted to carbon isotopes, ocean pH and temperatures, it rises from some 440 to some 7,390 ppm, about 36,000 billion tonnes of carbon, mostly the volcanoes’ own (Cui et al.). A lethally hot world. In the Early Triassic the tropical seas near 40 °C. Fish, many marine reptiles and calcareous algae are all but missing from the equator, and the land there was likely hotter still. Recovery, step by step. Life comes back slowly, held back by repeated crises, and complex ecosystems return only some five million years on, in the Middle Triassic.

passages.title: End-Triassic mass extinction
passages.text: One of the four marine extinctions that stand apart in the fossil record. The Central Atlantic Magmatic Province: lavas and sills over more than 7 million km² as first mapped, more than 10 million as known now, as Pangaea broke up, dated to the extinction. CO₂ about doubled after each of its first pulses, to some 4,400 ppm. The usual “Big Five” come from Raup & Sepkoski (1982), who found the Devonian’s stands out but not significantly. Bambach (2006) finds only three stand apart from the rest; Rampino & Shen (2019) add the end-Guadalupian as a sixth. Pangaea begins to break. Late in the Triassic, rifts open through the middle of Pangaea, where North America, Africa and South America meet: where the Atlantic will be. Magma underground first. Some 100,000 years before the first lavas, magma is already intruding the crust, and the climate and life begin to change with it. The lavas, and the extinction. The first flood lavas erupt as the extinction begins. In Brazil, sills spread through organic-rich rocks at the same time, their gas adding to the volcanoes’. Each eruption lasts a few centuries, carrying carbon dioxide from deep below, as much as this century’s projected human emissions. A burst of carbon, and warming. Within 10,000 to 20,000 years, at least 12,000 billion tonnes of light carbon, as methane, reach the air; the land warms and the rains grow heavier. Up to half the sea’s species are lost. Carbon dioxide doubles, and falls back. After the first lavas carbon dioxide rises from about 2,000 to about 4,400 ppm, then falls back over 300,000 years as fresh basalt weathers; the next two pulses do the same. Four pulses. The province erupts in four pulses over about 600,000 years, still erupting as life recovers. Its rocks are found today on four continents, over more than 7 million km² as first mapped (Marzoli et al.), over more than 10 million as known now (Lindström et al.). The age of dinosaurs. With their rivals gone, the dinosaurs come to dominate the land for the next 136 million years, and the Atlantic opens where the lavas poured out.

passages.title: End-Cretaceous extinction: the end of the dinosaurs
passages.text: The non-avian dinosaurs, the ammonites and most species of the time. The Chicxulub impact, widely held the main cause (Schulte et al.; Hull et al.). The Deccan Traps were erupting in India too: mostly before the impact (Schoene et al.) or after it (Sprain et al.), and how much that added is argued. The usual “Big Five” come from Raup & Sepkoski (1982), who found the Devonian’s stands out but not significantly. Bambach (2006) finds only three stand apart from the rest; Rampino & Shen (2019) add the end-Guadalupian as a sixth. Coming in. An asteroid over ten kilometres across comes in from the north-east, steeply, at tens of kilometres a second, over a shallow sea on the edge of what is now Yucatán. A fireball, and a hole in the crust. Within tens of seconds the impact opens a cavity about 100 km wide and some 30 km deep, and throws out a fireball and a plume of vaporised rock. The crater collapses. Within minutes the rock thrown up at the centre collapses outward into a ring of peaks, and the crater settles about 200 km across. The sea returns, and a tsunami. The sea rushes back over the peak ring within the hour. A tsunami runs across the Gulf and out into the oceans, scouring sea floors more than 10,000 km away. Ejecta fall round the world. Molten droplets thrown out of the crater fall back all round the Earth, a quarter within two hours, over half within eight, most within three days, heating the upper air as they come in. They leave the boundary layer found on every continent. Fires: how far they spread is disputed. Charcoal in the crater shows fires the impact set. Whether the heat lit fires worldwide is argued: yes, it was enough (Robertson et al.); no, the falling droplets shielded the ground (Goldin & Melosh), and live plants mostly would not ignite (Belcher et al.); in between, enough several thousand kilometres downrange (Morgan et al.). Acid rain. Sulfur from the vaporised anhydrite rock of the target turns to sulfuric acid, falling as acid rain within days. Darkness. Soot, dust and sulfate spread round the globe and block the sunlight: little or none reaches the surface for over a year, and photosynthesis all but stops for one to two. Which of them mattered most is disputed: soot (Bardeen et al.; Tabor et al.), fine silicate dust (Senel et al.), or sulfate (Brugger et al.). Impact winter. The continents cool by up to 28 °C and the oceans by up to 11 °C; middle latitudes stay below freezing for years: three to four with soot alone, three to sixteen in a model of the sulfate. The sky clears. The soot is gone after about five years; the climate takes decades to recover, more than thirty years in the sulfate model. A mass extinction. The non-avian dinosaurs, the ammonites and most species of the time are gone. The impact is widely held the main cause (Schulte et al.; Hull et al.). The Deccan Traps were erupting in India too: whether mostly before the impact (Schoene et al.) or after it (Sprain et al.), and how much that added, is argued. The oceans. The surface ocean acidified rapidly after the impact, then rebounded sharply. Plankton productivity came back within a few tens of thousands of years; the carrying of carbon to the deep sea took much longer. Life at ground zero. In the crater itself, life came back within years, and a thriving ecosystem within 30,000 years: faster than at many places far from it. Mammals and plants. On land, the number of mammal species doubles within about 100,000 years; by about 700,000 years larger mammals and the first legumes appear.
